2.text: Short socks, made of fawn-skin in mid-winter and of reindeer-leg skin in

3.text: other seasons, are similar in cut to the boots. They have the same strip

4.text: passing around the edge of the foot. They are always worn with the hair

5.text: side in, so that here again the boot and sock form the usual double article

6.text: of clothing. The Chukchee do not use for their socks very thick fawn-skin,

7.text: not even in the depth of winter, because it is supposed that a man keeps his

8.text: feet warm chiefly by motion. Indeed, a herdsman can use only thin leg-skin

9.text: socks, else his feet will perspire too much. As noted before, this lowers to a

10.text: considerable degree the protecting-power of clothes. A Yakut, when travelling

11.text: on horseback, requires extra covering for his feet, because they are exposed

12.text: to the cold from all sides. He therefore wears over the stockings of fawn-

13.text: skin short socks of the thick fluffy skin of the polar hare. His boots are

14.text: often made of the thick curried hide of a horse or an elk. Although these

15.text: are not so warm as leg-skin, they are better proof against dampness. Russian

16.text: merchants, officials, and other travellers wear double socks of thick fawn-skin.

17.text: Their boots are made of leg-skins, have soles of reindeer-sole, and thick grass

18.text: insoles. They are often extremely large. One pair in the collection has soles

19.text: 33 cm. long, 15 cm. wide, and 40 cm. around the foot, near the instep. Some-

20.text: times travellers wear over each boot a kind of furry bag to further protect

21.text: them from the cold. These are copied from the Tungus, who, when sleeping

22.text: in the open, protect their feet by this means.

23.text: Insoles of grass are used in all seasons, even with light summer boots,

24.text: which are worn without socks, because the native boots, with their thin, pliable

25.text: soles, are unfit to be worn without a grass insole. Tough, long-bladed grass

26.text: is selected for this purpose. The villages on the most exposed shores procure

27.text: this grass from the inland country by barter. Grass only partly dried is good

28.text: for insoles. In the fall women gather quantities of it to last their families

30.text: Boots with long legs, reaching to the knee and fastened over the trousers

31.text: with a gathering-string around the top, are often worn by men, although they

32.text: really belong to the woman’s attire. In many cases men wear them, on the

33.text: order of a shaman, as a means of concealing their identity, or at the bidding

34.text: of spirits, as the first step in transforming their individuality from male to

35.text: female.¹ Leggings of reindeer-leg skin are also used occasionally.

36.text: Mittens are made of reindeer-leg skin of various thicknesses. Their cut

37.text: is the same among all the tribes of northeastern Siberia (Fig. 172). Winter

38.text: gloves are almost unknown among the Chukchee. At present the Eskimo

39.text: women at Indian Point make very clumsy gloves in imitation of those of the

40.text: American whalers. The winter gloves that were formerly made were chiefly

41.text: connected with the performance of magic. Thus a very rude shamanistic

42.text: dress² has a left-hand glove attached to it.

43.text: ² Bogoras, Chukchee Materials, Plate II, Fig. 3.
